text.title: langchain-production-patterns Core Rules
text.summary: Hardening rules for production LangChain chains: fallbacks, retries, configurable fields, batch, dependency pinning, observability pairing.

rule.statement: Wire .with_fallbacks([backup]) when ≥2 providers are available AND target_uptime ≥ 0.99.
rule.rationale: Single-provider outages of 30-60min are routine; a non-fallback chain trips your SLA on the first one.

rule.statement: Cap retry.max_attempts at 5 with exponential backoff + jitter. Linear backoff or no cap turns a transient blip into a retry storm.
rule.rationale: Unbounded retries multiply load on the failing service, often making the outage worse and burning your budget.

rule.statement: Expose model + temperature via .configurable_fields so you can A/B and swap models at runtime without redeploy.
rule.rationale: Hot-swap saves you a deploy cycle when one model regresses.

rule.statement: Pin LangChain (and embedding model versions) to exact-hash via uv/pip-tools when dep_policy=locked. Minor releases have changed defaults in LangChain.
rule.rationale: Silent dep upgrades produced subtly different outputs the day after CI ran; only hash-pinning guarantees reproducibility.

rule.statement: Use chain.batch with return_exceptions=True; correlate results by input index, never by output order.
rule.rationale: Partial failures reorder outputs; downstream consumers assuming order silently see swapped results.

rule.statement: Alert when fallback hit-rate exceeds 5% over a 1-hour window. Silent successful fallback masks a dead primary.
rule.rationale: Fallbacks are safety nets, not free uptime; you need to know when they fire.

rule.statement: Pair every with_retry with an outer circuit breaker. Retries × tools = turn explosion otherwise (see [[max-turns-circuit-breaker]]).
rule.rationale: Tool-using agents amplify retry cost: each retry can spawn N more tool calls.

rule.statement: Require LangSmith tracing for every chain with fallbacks. Untraced fallbacks make root-cause analysis impossible.
rule.rationale: Without traces you cannot tell whether the primary or backup served the request, let alone why.

rule.statement: When the profile is valid, only one provider is available and latency_budget_ms is 500 or below, decision.fallbacks is empty and decision.retry MUST be max_attempts=1, backoff=none — no in-band retry at all. The patch instead wraps the LLM call in a circuit breaker that opens after a set number of consecutive failures, fails fast with a typed error while open, and half-opens after a cooldown; the failure threshold and cooldown are written into the hardening plan, and audit.rule_refs cites r7. A per-call timeout at or below the latency budget is mandatory so the breaker sees failures instead of hangs.

rationale.source: Nygard, Release It! (2nd ed., circuit breaker pattern); this methodology's Skip-If and 06-decision-tree

rule.rationale: At 500 ms a single retry with backoff already overruns the budget, so retrying converts a fast failure into a slow one and multiplies load on the provider that is struggling. Nygard's Release It! describes the circuit breaker as the pattern for exactly this case: stop calling a dependency that is failing, answer immediately, and probe it later, which keeps the latency promise while the provider recovers.

rule.statement: When the profile is valid, providers has 2 or more entries and target_uptime is 0.995 or higher, decision.fallbacks MUST list every non-primary provider in priority order AND at least one leg whose failure domain is not the primary's region (a second region of the same provider, or a second provider reached through a different region endpoint). The patch applies .with_retry to each leg and .with_fallbacks around them, in that order, so a transient error is retried on the primary before the chain fails over; the fallback hit-rate alert (r6) and tracing (r8) are wired in the same patch, and audit.rule_refs cites r1, r6 and r8.

rationale.source: LangChain documentation (Runnable.with_fallbacks, Runnable.with_retry); this methodology's 04-procedure step 2

rule.rationale: 99.5% leaves about 3.6 hours of downtime a month; a single provider outage of 30-60 minutes fits, a regional incident that takes the provider's API down for an afternoon does not, and a second provider in the same region can share the incident. LangChain's Runnable docs define with_fallbacks as trying alternatives in order on exception, which is only worth anything if the alternative can fail independently.

rule.statement: When the profile is valid, providers has 2 or more entries and target_uptime is below 0.995, decision.fallbacks MUST name at least one backup provider in priority order, single-region; a cross-region leg is optional and its extra latency is not charged against latency_budget_ms. Retry follows the latency band from 04-procedure step 3 (max_attempts 2, 3 or 5) and wraps each leg before .with_fallbacks; the fallback hit-rate alert (r6) still applies, and audit.rule_refs cites r1 and r6.

rationale.source: LangChain documentation (Runnable.with_fallbacks); this methodology's 04-procedure steps 2 and 3

rule.rationale: Below 99.5% the SLA tolerates one provider incident a month, so a second provider covers the failure shape that actually occurs — the primary's API down for under an hour — and a cross-region topology buys resilience the target never asked for at the price of a slower fallback path. The alert stays because a backup that silently serves 100% of traffic is a dead primary nobody noticed.

rule.statement: When the profile is valid, only one provider is available and latency_budget_ms is above 500, decision.fallbacks is empty and decision.retry MUST be backoff=exponential with jitter (with_retry(wait_exponential_jitter=True)), max_attempts=3 for a 500-2000 ms budget and 5 above 2000 ms, never more. Retries MUST be limited to transient failures (rate limit, timeout, 5xx) via retry_if_exception_type, so a 4xx from a bad prompt is not retried, and the whole retry chain sits inside the outer circuit breaker required by r7; audit.rule_refs cites r2 and r7.

rationale.source: Brooker 2015, Exponential Backoff and Jitter (AWS Architecture Blog); LangChain documentation (Runnable.with_retry)

rule.rationale: With no second provider the only lever is time, and exponential backoff with jitter is the strategy that spreads retries instead of synchronising every client onto the recovering service (Brooker, "Exponential Backoff and Jitter", AWS Architecture Blog, 2015). Retrying a deterministic 400 five times is five bills for one bug, which is why the exception filter is part of the rule, not a nicety.
